concept: Data Federation over customer S3 with partitioning
summary: Source-anchored research for Data Federation over customer S3 with partitioning. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Partition-key predicates are a general scan-control pattern across object-store query engines: AWS Athena describes pruning S3 partitions that do not match query predicates, and Trino's Hive connector documents dynamic partition pruning and an optional requirement for partition filters. These are cross-engine context and do not mean Athena or Trino settings apply to Atlas Data Federation. (medium confidence)

Data Federation adds partition attributes even when a stored document already has a field with the same name, creating duplicate field names that MongoDB does not support. Use distinct partition names or `omitAttributes`; a community user also reported that renaming a colliding field resolved their partition query issue. (high confidence)

Give path partition attributes names that do not collide with fields inside the documents. Atlas warns that it adds path attributes even when a same-named document field exists, creating duplicate field names; a 2023 community report said renaming a colliding ObjectId path attribute restored query filtering. (medium confidence)

Avoid layouts that create many small files or excessive partitions. MongoDB says many small files compound per-file resource use and large files can require unnecessary downloads; AWS Athena separately warns that too many S3 partitions add file and partition-filtering overhead, while too few can increase scans. (high confidence)

Selective partition matches can reduce Data Federation's processed bytes and charges, but partitioning does not guarantee savings: a query that reads the whole collection still processes the whole collection. MongoDB's example contrasts reading one 1 GB partition from a 10 GB file layout with processing all 10 GB when no partition can be skipped. (high confidence)
MongoDB's billing page lists Data Federation processing at $5 per TB with a 10 MB minimum per query. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-18)

MongoDB recommends ordering S3 partition fields from the most frequently queried to the least frequently queried. A query that skips an earlier path field can use matching earlier partitions more efficiently than later ones; fields absent from the configured path cannot prune files. (high confidence)

For customer-managed S3, a collection's `dataSources.path` can map S3 key segments to computed partition attributes, and predicates on those attributes can target matching prefixes and files. Independent OneUptime and Medium write-ups describe the same path-to-field and filter pattern, but provide no measured benchmark. (medium confidence)

Atlas Data Federation maps configured S3 stores to virtual databases and collections. Its data-source path syntax can parse key or filename segments into typed partition attributes and add those attributes to query documents. (high confidence)

Atlas charges separately for data processed and data returned or transferred. A filter on mapped S3 path attributes can target matching files and reduce processed bytes, but a broad query such as a blank $match still reads the full collection, so partitioning alone does not guarantee lower processing cost. (high confidence)
